newsitem.title: UK: Copper pushes higher, lifts other metals.
newsitem.headline: Copper pushes higher, lifts other metals.

text.p: Buoyant world copper prices helped fuel rallies in other industrial metals on Wednesday.

Copper, the London Metal Exchange's (LME) flagship contract, hit a new five-month peak at 2,240-a-tonne, extending a rally that began late last week. Prices were boosted largely by data suggesting that stocks were at their lowest in six years.
Copper had broken through the $2,200 barrier on Monday.

It eased from the highs in later Wednesday trading but stayed above that level. Traders reported market talk that a long run of inventory declines, which has brought LME copper stocks to the lowest since June 1990, may be coming to an end.
The explosive copper rally spurred other key base metals to rise. Aluminium rose above $1,500 a tonne to hit $1,505 -- its higest for 2-1/2 months -- as consumers returned to that market.
"Everything seems to be bubbling along led by copper," said Angus MacMillan, analyst at LME broker Billiton Metals Ltd.

Aluminium, used in construction and the transport industry, gained $20 despite a report by the International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI) that average daily output by the major producers rose in October.
Despite some profit-taking and late sell-offs, it ended the London afternoon kerb at $1,508 per tonne.
Speculators were also attracted to zinc, used in galvanising steel. Three month zinc futures hit $1,082 a tonne bid early on Wednesday, at the highest level for 6-1/2 months.

Traders said falling stocks and strong sentiment were triggering trade and fund-related buying. The market was helped by Spanish producer Asturiana de Zinc's recent confirmation that it had offloaded a long futures position which traders said had been constraining prices in the last few years.
On Tuesday LME zinc stocks fell to 534,750 tonnes, the lowest level since February 1993.
In the precious metals, gold and silver notched higher in the afternoon, bolstered by news of a wider-than-expected U.S. trade gap in September. Gold closed in London at $379.15 per ounce.
In the soft commodities, cocoa burst out of a negative trend in a fierce rally, clearing the way for more gains.
A strong close on the benchmark cocoa suggested the market may have secured its position above a downtrend channel that had kept a stiff lid on gains in the last month.
Helped by follow-through buying in New York, London March cocoa jumped to a session high of 931 pounds sterling a tonne, then closed slightly lower at 928 sterling, up 15 stg on the day.
